prompts.question: Describe the advantages and limitations of using quantitative data in a research project.
markerNotes: Describe each point in terms of the research, not only its label: say why numerical results are easy to compare, or why a number cannot show the reasons behind an answer.
Advantages that earn credit link to the purpose of the research, such as numbers from a large sample can be compared and the research repeated, which supports reliability.
Limitations should say what the data cannot show, such as depth or the reasons for responses, rather than that the data is weak.
commonStudentErrors: Describing qualitative data, or the sources of data, when the question asks about quantitative data.
Listing advantages and limitations as single words without describing how each one affects the research.
Calling quantitative data more accurate or better without saying why.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Provides a sound description of the advantages and limitations of using quantitative data in a research project
3 marks: Provides some description of the advantages and limitations of using quantitative data in a research project
2 marks: Demonstrates a limited understanding of the advantage(s) and/or disadvantage(s) of quantitative data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
In a research project, the advantages of using quantitative data include:
• Sample sizes can be collated and analysed easily by comparing numbers
• Research can be repeated which increases reliability.
The limitations of using quantitative data include:
• Data lacks in-depth answers
• The why/reasons for answers are not included.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes an advantage (numbers can be collated and compared easily) and a limitation (the reasons for answers are missing), each in a sound sentence. The answer is brief and well matched to 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Quantitative data can be counted and compared easily. A limitation is that it does not show why people answered as they did.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: names an advantage and a limitation with limited understanding, and neither is developed. Explaining how the advantage helps the research would move it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Quantitative data uses numbers, such as counts from a survey.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about quantitative data, but no advantage or limitation is given. Naming one advantage would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: A researcher has chosen to investigate the opinions of adults about changes to social media use by young people 16 years and under. Discuss the suitability of TWO research methods for this research topic.
markerNotes: Name two methods and judge how suitable each is for this topic, which asks for the opinions of adults and so calls for qualitative data.
Weigh each method strengths against its limitations for this topic, not in general terms; an interview gathers depth but needs many interviews to represent adults.
Discussion needs a point on each side for each method; a one-sided account of either method does not discuss it.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the two methods without judging how suitable they are for adults' opinions.
Discussing research methods in general rather than their suitability for this topic.
Choosing a closed survey and calling it suitable without considering how far it captures opinions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides an extensive discussion of the suitability of TWO research methods for this research topic
5 marks: Provides a thorough discussion of the suitability of TWO research methods for this research topic
4 marks: Provides a sound discussion of the suitability of TWO research methods for this research topic
3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of research methods for this research topic
2 marks: Provides some information of research methods and/or for this research topic
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
This research topic is seeking subjective data to learn about adults’ opinions on the topic and must use methodologies that predominantly collect qualitative data. Interviews can collect a cross section of opinions, however a larger number of interviews will need to take place, otherwise this could create bias.
A case study is a detailed and in-depth investigation. It is suitable for this topic as it allows a detailed picture to be formed concerning changes to social media for young people, making the why and how of research clearer. However, it is time-consuming as there are multiple steps, and the large amount of data collected can be difficult to compile and present.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: discusses the suitability of two methods for adults' opinions on this topic, with a strength and a limitation for each. The case study point links the method detail to the need for a clear picture of the issue.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interviews can gather adults' opinions in depth, but a small number may not represent everyone's views.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: some understanding of one method and its suitability, with a single point and no second method. Adding a second method and its limits would move it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A survey could be used to ask adults about social media.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about a method, with no judgement of its suitability. Judging why a survey suits or does not suit opinions would lift it to the 3-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify steps that would address the research issue presented in the diary.
markerNotes: Identify the issue the diary reveals first, then justify each step by what it fixes; here the target group did not answer under the same conditions, so the results are unreliable.
A justified step says what it fixes and why that makes the research more reliable, such as a set time for everyone and clear instructions.
A step that repeats a problem from the diary without changing it does not address the issue.
commonStudentErrors: Proposing steps without saying why each one addresses the issue in the diary.
Describing the problems in the diary rather than proposing solutions to them.
Suggesting the researcher should do better without a specific change, such as a new time or clearer instructions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Justifies steps to address the research issue presented in the diary
4 marks: Justifies some steps to address the research issue presented in the diary
3 marks: Provides some steps to address the research issue
2 marks: Demonstrates a basic understanding of the issue and/or solutions
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The whole target sample was not able to answer the questionnaire under the same or similar conditions, therefore the research method was unreliable. To solve this issue:
• Set a new time for the whole target group to complete the questionnaire.
• Deliver the instructions for the questionnaire, stating confidentiality to reassure participants.
By setting a new time, a clear process can be followed with enough time to read and answer the questions, give consent, and ensure the process can be repeated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: justifies two steps, a new time and clear instructions with confidentiality, and ties each to the reliability of the research. The answer also explains why a set time lets the process be repeated.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hold the questionnaire again at a set time, and give clear instructions to everyone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: provides two steps that address the issue but gives no justification for either. Explaining why each step makes the results more reliable would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The questionnaire was poorly organised, so the researcher should plan it better.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about the issue, but the step is too general to address it. A specific step, such as a set time, would move it to the 3-mark row.

prompts.question: Explain how aspects of services can affect rural and remote families’ access to the services.
markerNotes: Name one aspect of the service, such as opening hours, location, staffing or confidentiality, and explain how it limits access for rural and remote families.
Connect each aspect to the family situation, such as farm work or long travel, so the explanation shows the effect rather than the feature.
Explaining two aspects in depth separates a sound answer from one that only lists aspects.
commonStudentErrors: Describing services in remote areas without naming an aspect of the service that affects access.
Explaining the difficulties of rural life in general rather than how aspects of services affect access.
Naming location or staffing as a problem without saying why it matters for the family.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Provides a comprehensive explanation of how aspects of services can affect rural and remote families’ access to services
6 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of how aspects of services can affect rural and remote families’ access to services

sampleAnswers.answer:
Staffing – rural and remote areas are more likely to experience a skills shortage. For acute health issues such as crush farming injuries, there may not be trained or experienced staff. Online financial support services can be accessed when convenient, however if metropolitan based, they may lack knowledge of remote issues, such as drought specific rebates.
Confidentiality – keeping personal matters private can be challenging due to the size of communities. In smaller communities, family members may be less likely to disclose sensitive but necessary health information to health services, for fear of judgement or shame, leading to worsening health condition.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains how staffing and confidentiality affect access for rural and remote families, with a clear reason for each. Both aspects are developed fully, which is what the top row asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rural families may find services are open only during business hours, which clashes with work on the farm. Travel to services can also be costly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: a sound explanation of one aspect, with the second aspect named but not explained. Developing the travel point, such as the time and cost to the family, would lift it to the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Services in the country are often far away, so families have to drive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: some understanding of a feature of services and its effect, but the explanation is brief and the aspect is not named. Explaining why distance limits access, such as the time and fuel cost, would move it up.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Group: Homeless people
Orange Sky is a community organisation that supports the rights of homeless people to access basic health and hygiene. Some homeless people are rough sleepers, using makeshift dwellings like tents, derelict buildings or cars and have limited access to shower and laundry facilities. This organisation has easily distinguishable orange vans containing shower and laundry facilities, that frequent known areas of rough sleepers. This means the members of this group can wash and feel clean, reducing risk of infection, and can have their clothes cleaned and dried.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains how a named organisation gives homeless people access to a basic right, with the reason its vans reach rough sleepers. The explanation stays on the question and links the service to the group wellbeing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Orange Sky is a community organisation that gives homeless people access to showers and laundry, so they can keep clean.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: shows one way a named organisation supports the group, but does not explain how this supports a right. Explaining the effect on the group health would move it to the 4-mark row.

prompts.question: Answer the question in relation to ONE of the following Category B groups. To what extent does legislation ensure equity for the diverse members within this group? Use specific examples of legislation to support your answer.
markerNotes: Judge the extent: say how far the legislation delivers equity and where it falls short, then take a position rather than describing the Act.
Diversity within the group is what the question tests; show that the legislation helps some members more than others, such as by type of disability.
Name the legislation accurately and link each Act to a specific effect on equity, with an example of how it works in practice.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what the legislation says without judging how far it ensures equity.
Treating the group as one uniform group and ignoring the diversity within it.
Listing several Acts without explaining what each one does for equity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Provides valid judgement on the extent to which legislation ensures equity for the diversity within one of the groups; Provides detailed examples
6-7 marks: Provides judgement on the extent to which legislation ensures equity for the diversity within one of the groups; Provides relevant examples
4-5 marks: Attempts to provide judgement on how legislation contributes to equity and/or diversity within one of the groups; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of legislation in relation to equity and/or diversity within one of the groups
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Group: People with disabilities
The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (DDA) makes it unlawful to discriminate against a person based on disability in many areas of life, including the workplace. The broad definition of a disability can impact the identification of and successful implementation of reasonable adjustments to support inclusion.
For those with a physical disability that can be seen visually, installing ramps can be understood and easily implemented without judgement, increasing equity of access. For those with a psychosocial disability or illness, the nature of the workplace adjustment such as flexible work arrangements may inadvertently lead colleagues to gossip, ask questions and speculate, which may lead to indirect discrimination. Therefore, the DDA may have some success in creating equity. However, there is still considerable inequity across the diversity of the group based on an individual’s disability category.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: makes a valid judgement that the Disability Discrimination Act creates some equity but leaves inequity across disability types, supported by detailed examples of ramps and psychosocial disability. The judgement is clear and is returned to in the final sentence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legislation such as the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 makes it unlawful to discriminate against people with disability at work and in other areas. For example, an employer may need to make reasonable adjustments. This helps some people with disability, but not all of them, so the law is only partly effective.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: attempts a judgement on how the legislation contributes to equity, with an example. The judgement is stated but not supported, and the diversity within the group is not explored. Explaining why the law helps a physical disability more than a psychosocial one would move it up.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legislation such as the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 protects people with disability from unfair treatment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: some understanding of legislation and equity for the group, but no judgement and no example. Adding an example of how the Act works in practice would move it to the 4-5 row.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Culture, customs and traditions shape the values that parents and carers pass on, so they affect how children are raised and how dependants are cared for. Cultural values about family roles influence parenting style. In some families, parents expect children to show respect to elders and to follow adults' decisions, so a parent may use a firm, directive approach, which resembles an authoritarian style. In other families, cultural values encourage children to contribute ideas, which supports a more democratic style that builds a child's confidence.

Customs set the routines of family life, and these routines strengthen bonds between family members. A family that shares meals or attends a weekly religious service together builds a sense of belonging, and children learn social norms through these routines. Traditions passed down through generations, such as language, dress and cooking, preserve cultural identity. A grandparent who teaches a grandchild their first language strengthens the relationship between the generations, although traditions can also create tension when they conflict with the expectations of school or the wider community.

Culture also shapes caring. In many families, care for an ageing parent or grandparent is seen as a duty of the family, so relatives may provide care at home rather than use formal services. This affects how much support the carer seeks from outside, and it can add to the carer's own pressure when that duty is not shared.

sampleAnswers.answer: Culture affects parenting because parents pass on their values to their children. For example, a family with strong religious beliefs may attend services together, which teaches children about their faith. Traditions such as speaking a home language also shape how children see their identity, although the language may be harder to use at school.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Government legislation and entitlements address many current issues for older people, but they do not resolve them all. Their main strength is that they set out the rights of the aged and provide income and in-home support. Their limitation is that they respond unevenly to issues that law cannot easily solve, such as housing costs and social isolation, so some older people's wellbeing is still at risk.

The Aged Care Act 2024 places the rights of older people at the centre of the aged care system. It aims to make the system simpler, with supported decision making, so that services are safe and of high quality. This responds to the serious failings identified by the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety, whose final report in 2021 called for major change. The Act improves wellbeing by setting clear standards, but a standard on paper does not guarantee a suitable place in a facility for every older person who needs one.

Many older people prefer to remain in their own homes, and the Support at Home Program is designed to help them do this. It can fund specialist services and home modifications, which allows an older person to stay healthy, happy and safe at home for longer. This addresses the issue of independence directly. Its effect depends on the availability of workers and on the older person's ability to navigate the system, so people with limited digital skills or family support may gain less from it.

The Age Discrimination Act 2004 makes it unlawful to treat a person unfairly because of their age, which targets ageism in employment, services and the community. This protects the wellbeing of older people who want to keep working or take part in community life. However, the law relies on individuals making complaints, and many older people may not do so, particularly if they depend on the person they would complain about.

Government entitlements, especially the Age Pension, reduce financial hardship. For many older people the pension is a main source of income, and it helps with the costs of housing, food and health care. It supports wellbeing by reducing financial stress. Yet the pension does not solve the housing affordability problem that many older renters face, and no entitlement can by itself prevent loneliness or social isolation.

Overall, government legislation and entitlements address current issues for the aged to a considerable extent, because they protect rights, support independent living and provide income. They do less well on issues such as housing costs and social isolation, which have a direct effect on wellbeing but depend on communities and families as much as on law. The extent of their success therefore depends on whether the services that legislation promises are actually delivered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: extensive knowledge of the Aged Care Act 2024, the Support at Home Program, the Age Discrimination Act and the Age Pension, a judgement on the extent to which they address current issues, and clear links to wellbeing. The verdict is qualified by what the measures cannot do, which keeps it well informed.

The Age Pension gives older people an income, which helps them meet everyday costs. The Age Discrimination Act 2004 also protects older people from unfair treatment because of age. Support at Home helps older people stay in their own homes, so they can remain independent for longer. However, many older people still struggle with housing costs, and the legislation does not directly address this. Loneliness is another issue that a payment cannot fix. Overall, legislation and entitlements help the aged to some extent, but they do not address every current issue.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Emerging technologies in transport and medicine improve the wellbeing of many individuals, but the benefits are uneven and several ethical questions remain unresolved. Judged against the criteria of safety, equity and access, and ethics, the impact is strongest where a technology reduces risk or cost for many people at once, and weakest where it creates new risks that the law has not yet addressed.

In transport, autonomous vehicles are the clearest example. Their advanced sensors aim to reduce road accidents, which directly improves physical wellbeing by making travel safer for passengers, pedestrians and other drivers. They may also widen access for people who cannot drive, such as some people with disability and some older people, which supports independence and participation in community life. The ethical problems are serious, however. A vehicle may face a situation in which every option causes harm, and there is no agreed standard for how it should choose. The cost of the technology may also mean that its benefits go mainly to people who can afford new vehicles. Lighter and more fuel-efficient aircraft engines show a similar pattern: they reduce airline costs and can make cheaper flights available, which helps people on lower incomes travel, but greater access does not necessarily improve the wellbeing of every traveller.

In medicine, telehealth and new diagnostic tools expand access to care. Telehealth lets people in rural and remote areas consult a doctor without a long journey, which reduces the time, cost and fatigue of travel. The vaccines developed during the COVID-19 pandemic reduced severe illness and allowed people to return to their daily lives. Where they were free and easy to reach at pharmacies and general practices, they show how a technology can be shared fairly. Reproductive technologies such as IVF have given many people the chance of parenthood, but they raise difficult ethical questions. The fertility industry has been criticised for lacking consistent national regulation, which has allowed a single donor to father many donor-conceived children. This affects the wellbeing of those children and their families, and shows that the benefits depend on the regulation that accompanies a technology.

Overall, emerging technologies in transport and medicine have a positive impact on the wellbeing of individuals, particularly where they make travel and care safer and more accessible. Their impact is less clear where ethical and equity questions remain open, such as the decisions an autonomous vehicle makes in a crash and the regulation of donor conception. The judgement is therefore favourable but conditional: the technology improves wellbeing when governments and industry manage its risks and share its benefits fairly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: extensive knowledge of autonomous vehicles and medical technologies, a well-informed judgement against stated criteria, and clear links to the wellbeing of individuals in both contexts. The verdict is conditional and argued, which is what separates an evaluation from a list.

sampleAnswers.answer: Emerging technologies in transport and medicine have a mostly positive impact on individuals. Autonomous vehicles use sensors to reduce road accidents, which improves physical safety, and they may help people who cannot drive. Aircraft engines that burn less fuel can make cheaper flights available. However, autonomous vehicles raise ethical issues about how they should act in a crash, and the technology may be expensive, so not everyone benefits. In medicine, telehealth allows people in remote areas to see a doctor without travelling, which improves access to care. Reproductive technologies such as IVF bring benefits to families but also ethical concerns, because the fertility industry has been criticised for lacking consistent national regulation. Overall, these technologies improve wellbeing for many people, but the benefits are not shared equally and the ethical questions are not fully answered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: sound knowledge of autonomous vehicles, telehealth and reproductive technologies, with an example for each and a link to wellbeing. The overall judgement is stated but not argued against criteria, and the equity point is brief. Testing the benefits against equity and ethics in more depth would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Shift and part-time work support many young people to manage multiple roles, but how far they do so depends on the hours, how predictable they are, and the young person's health. Young people often combine study at university or TAFE, paid work, caring for younger siblings or an ageing grandparent, sport, volunteering and their social life. A job that can be arranged around these commitments supports wellbeing; one that cannot adds to the strain.

Part-time work offers the greatest flexibility. A young person can work a few hours a week around a timetable of lectures or classes, and entitlements such as leave are paid pro rata, so the work still carries workplace rights. Part-time roles in retail, hairdressing, landscaping and real estate allow young people to gain workplace skills without giving up their studies. However, part-time work is not always predictable. Employers may change rosters at short notice, which makes it hard to plan caring responsibilities or study, and fewer hours mean a lower income.

Shift work responds to a different need. It is performed outside the typical 9 to 5 working day, in roles such as hospitality, bar work, event promotion and music festivals. Evening and weekend shifts may attract extra pay, and they can suit a student whose classes are in the morning. Shift work also meets social needs, because young people working at a bar or festival are part of a peer group. The trade-off is that night and irregular hours can disturb sleep. Poor sleep affects concentration for study and can make it harder to look after younger siblings, so the roles that shift work is meant to support may compete with one another.

The support depends on the young person's circumstances. A young person caring for a grandparent may not be able to sustain evening shifts, while a young person with few other commitments may manage them easily. Those who can negotiate hours, swap shifts or choose a regular roster are better placed to balance their roles than those who must accept whatever the employer offers.

Overall, shift and part-time work support young people to manage multiple roles to a considerable extent, particularly when hours are regular, pay is fair and the young person keeps some control over when they work. Part-time work is more likely to protect wellbeing because it is easier to plan around, while shift work can help a young person meet study and social needs at the cost of health if sleep is repeatedly disrupted. The support is therefore conditional rather than automatic.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: extensive knowledge of how shift and part-time work relate to young people, a well-informed judgement on the extent of support with its conditions, and clear links to the wellbeing of young people. The two patterns are distinguished throughout, which keeps the response logical and cohesive.

sampleAnswers.answer: Part-time work helps many young people manage multiple roles because it provides fewer hours and more flexibility. For example, a student can work a few shifts a week around university classes, and the entitlements are paid pro rata. Shift work, such as bar work or hospitality, suits young people who want to earn money and see friends, but night work can cause sleep problems, which affects study. Young people who care for others may find irregular shifts hard to manage. Overall, shift and part-time work support multiple roles for some young people but not all, depending on their circumstances.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: sound knowledge of how part-time and shift work relate to young people, with examples and a link to managing multiple roles. sampleAnswers.answer:
Technology such as advancements in the speed of the internet have led to competitive international job markets. Businesses can communicate 24 hours per day meaning that past full time permanent employment has led to the emergence of shift work and the flexibility of working remotely.
As the economy changes from high prosperity to a recession, work patterns change. When the economy is experiencing a high such as a boom, employees can confidently negotiate from full time work to flexible work patterns, such as working remotely or start businesses and becoming self-employed. Employees benefit from higher wages and flexibility, managing work life balance.
